results.content: # Assessing Gain and Phase Margins. This example shows how to examine the effect of stability margins on closed-loop response characteristics of a control system. ### Stability of a Feedback Loop. For linear feedback systems, stability can be assessed by looking at the poles of the closed-loop transfer function. For a unit loop gain `k`, you can compute the closed-loop transfer function `T` using:. The feedback loop for `k=1` is stable since all poles have negative real parts. One indication of robustness is how much the loop gain can change before stability is lost. This range shows that with `k=1`, the loop gain can increase 270% before you lose stability. ### Gain and Phase Margins. Changes in the loop gain are only one aspect of robust stability. Because modeling errors are most damaging near the gain crossover frequency (frequency where open-loop gain is 0dB), it also matters how much phase variation can be tolerated at this frequency. The phase margin measures how much phase variation is needed at the gain crossover frequency to lose stability. Similarly, the gain margin measures what relative gain variation is needed at the phase crossover frequency to lose stability. Together, these two numbers give an estimate of the "safety margin" for closed-loop stability. You can display the gain and phase margins on a Bode plot as follows. Then, right-click on the plot and select the **Characteristics -> Minimum Stability Margins** submenu. results.title: Dynamical Response Properties of Neocortical Neuron Ensembles: Multiplicative versus Additive Noise | Journal of Neuroscience
results.content: We injected sinusoidally modulated noisy currents (additive and multiplicative modulation) into layer V pyramidal neurons of the rat somatosensory cortex and measured the trial and ensemble-averaged spike responses for a wide range of stimulus frequencies. For additive input modulation, it has been demonstrated that ensembles of neocortical neurons can track stimuli in the presence of colored noise very fast: up to frequencies of 200 Hz (Köndgen et al., 2008). Synaptic input currents *I*(*t*) were synthesized as Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise *z*(*t*) (i.e., low-pass filtered white noise *x*(*t*), τ · *dz* / *dt* = −*z*(*t*) + *x*(*t*), time constant τ = 1 ms) with a sinusoidal modulation of the mean (additive modulation), or of the variance of the noise (multiplicative modulation), Four different modulation depths (*I* 1 = 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1) and modulation frequencies ranging from 1–1000 Hz were used. To test for the presence of transmission delays d between input currents and spike responses, we fitted a linear decay, to the phase of the population averaged transfer function at high frequencies (800–1000 Hz). Dependence of low-frequency gain *H* 0 ( ***A*** ), cutoff frequency *f* c ( ***B*** ), decay exponent α ( ***C*** ) and transmission delay *d* ( ***D*** ) on stimulus amplitude *I* 1 for additive (gray) and multiplicative (black) modulation. Since neocortical neurons in acute brain slices are usually not spontaneously active, we scaled the injected noisy currents appropriately to keep the average firing rates *r* 0 in a low narrow range (Fig. 1 *B*) (7 ± 3 spikes/s for additive modulation, 5 ± 3 spikes/s for multiplicative modulation). 2, 3, thin gray lines) shows that for small stimulus amplitudes (*I* 1 = 0.1) individual cells could reliably track the stimuli up to frequencies of ∼200 Hz for both the additive (Fig. 2 *A*) and the multiplicative (Fig. 3 *A*) modulation scheme. For multiplicative modulation with large modulation depths (*I* 1 = 0.5, 1.0), we observe reliable population responses up to 1 kHz. Note, that these data were obtained for a small population of *N* cells by averaging over many stimulus periods over a rather long, physiologically nonrelevant, time window of *T* = 50 s.
